Holiday Club Scam UK: How to Spot and Avoid Timeshare Fraud

Holiday club scams promise the world but deliver debt — here's how to recognise and avoid them.

By Alex Bacsa · Published 2026-07-08 · 9 min read

holiday club scam UKtimeshare scam UKholiday membership fraudfake holiday clubholiday scam warning signs
Key rule: verify through an official route you opened yourself, not the link, number, app, or payment details supplied by the suspicious message.

Being targeted right now? Do this

  1. Stop. Don’t pay, transfer money, or share passwords, PINs, or one-time codes.
  2. Contact your bank on the number on the back of your card if your money or details may be at risk.
  3. Report it — call Action Fraud on 0300 123 2040 (Police Scotland: 101), and forward scam texts to 7726.

What is a holiday club scam?

A holiday club scam is a fraudulent scheme that poses as a legitimate membership organisation offering discounted holidays, exclusive resort access, or travel deals. Scammers contact you by phone, email, or in person at travel shows, claiming you've won a free holiday or qualified for a special offer. They pressure you to attend a high-pressure sales presentation, where they push you to sign up for an expensive annual membership or buy into a timeshare-style scheme. The promised holidays are either non-existent, vastly overpriced, or come with so many hidden fees and restrictions that they offer no real saving.

Once you've signed the contract and paid an upfront fee (often hundreds or thousands of pounds), the company becomes difficult to contact, refuses refunds, or continues charging you for years. The scam exploits people's desire for affordable holidays and relies on aggressive sales tactics, misleading claims about the value of membership, and deliberately confusing contract terms.

Warning signs of a holiday club scam

  • You are contacted out of the blue by phone, email, or text claiming you've won a free holiday or special offer — legitimate holiday companies do not cold-call or email random people with unsolicited deals.
  • The offer sounds too good to be true: heavily discounted holidays, exclusive access to luxury resorts, or membership at a fraction of the normal price — scammers use unrealistic promises to hook you.
  • You are pressured to attend a sales presentation or 'information session' urgently, with language like 'limited time only' or 'spaces filling fast' — genuine holiday companies do not use artificial urgency to force attendance.
  • The company asks for an upfront payment before you can access any holidays or see the full contract terms — legitimate travel services do not demand money before you understand what you're buying.
  • The contract is long, complex, and full of small print that contradicts the verbal promises made during the sales pitch — scammers deliberately obscure the true cost and terms.
  • You are told you can cancel 'anytime' but the contract actually locks you in for years with heavy cancellation fees — this is a classic bait-and-switch tactic.
  • The company is difficult to contact after you've paid, or staff become evasive when you ask questions about refunds or cancellation — legitimate businesses have accessible customer service.
  • Reviews online are either non-existent, overwhelmingly negative, or suspiciously positive with generic language — scammers often have no real customer feedback or fake reviews.

How the scam unfolds from first contact to payment

The scam typically begins with an unsolicited phone call, email, or text message claiming you've won a free holiday, qualified for an exclusive deal, or been selected for a special membership offer. The scammer may pose as a representative of a travel company, holiday club, or resort group, and will use high-pressure sales language to convince you to attend a 'presentation' or 'information session'. Once you arrive at the venue (often a hotel conference room or travel show booth), you are seated with a salesperson who presents glossy brochures and testimonials, emphasising the 'incredible value' and 'exclusive benefits' of membership.

They will claim you can book luxury holidays at a fraction of normal prices, access resorts worldwide, or enjoy lifetime travel benefits. The salesperson will then pressure you to sign a contract immediately, using tactics like 'this offer expires today' or 'we only have a few memberships left'. They will downplay or obscure the true cost, the length of the commitment, and the cancellation terms. Once you sign and hand over payment (by card, bank transfer, or cheque), the company either disappears, becomes unresponsive, or continues charging you annual fees while delivering little or no value.

Many victims discover too late that the promised holidays are either unavailable, require additional payments, or are booked at inflated prices that negate any saving.

How to verify if a holiday club offer is genuine

Before attending any presentation or handing over money, take these steps to check if the company is legitimate. First, search the company name online along with the words 'scam', 'complaint', or 'review' — if there are numerous complaints about high-pressure sales, hidden fees, or refusal to cancel, it is almost certainly a scam. Check the company's registration with Companies House (companieshouse.gov.uk) — a genuine UK travel company should be registered and have a clear business address and history.

Look for contact details on their website: a legitimate company will have a physical UK address, a working phone number, and a named customer service team. Call the number on their official website (not a number given to you by a salesperson) and ask specific questions about cancellation terms, total cost, and what holidays are actually available — scammers will be evasive or contradictory.

Check if they are a member of a recognised travel industry body such as ABTA (Association of British Travel Agents) or ATOL (Air Travel Organisers' Licensing) — membership is a sign of legitimacy, though not a guarantee. Be extremely wary of any company that pressures you to attend a presentation, demands upfront payment before showing you the full contract, or refuses to provide written terms in advance. If you are unsure, contact Citizens Advice (0808 223 1133) or check the NCSC website for warnings about specific companies.

What to do immediately if you have already paid

If you have signed a contract and paid money to a holiday club, act quickly. First, stop any further payments immediately — contact your bank or card provider and ask them to block any recurring charges or standing orders to the company. Second, request a full refund in writing (email or letter) to the company's registered address, citing the Consumer Rights Act 2015 and your right to cancel within 14 days if you are a consumer (this applies even if you signed in person). Keep a copy of this request.

Third, check your bank or credit card statement for the transaction and gather all documents: the contract, emails, receipts, and any promotional materials you were given. Fourth, if the company refuses to refund you or becomes unresponsive, contact your bank's dispute team and ask about a chargeback — your bank can recover the money if the company has not delivered what was promised. Fifth, report the scam to Action Fraud (0300 123 2040) and provide them with all evidence. If you paid by card and suspect fraud, you can also report it to your card provider's fraud team.

Do not send any more money to the company, and do not sign any additional documents they send you.

Reporting a holiday club scam in the UK

Report the scam to Action Fraud, the UK's national fraud reporting service, by calling 0300 123 2040 or visiting actionfraud.police.uk. Provide them with the company name, contact details, the date you were contacted, how much money you paid, and copies of any contracts, emails, or promotional materials. Action Fraud will log your report and may investigate if there is a pattern of complaints. If you received the initial contact by email or text, forward it to the NCSC Suspicious Email Reporting Service at report@phishing.gov.uk — this helps them track and block phishing and scam messages.

If you received a spam text, forward it to 7726 (free of charge) — this alerts your mobile network to the scam. Contact Citizens Advice (0808 223 1133) for free guidance on your consumer rights and whether you have grounds for a refund or chargeback. If the company is registered at Companies House, you can also report concerns to the Insolvency Service or request a strike-off if the company is no longer trading legitimately. Keep detailed records of all your reports and correspondence — this will help if you need to pursue a chargeback or small claims action later.

Do not delay reporting; the sooner Action Fraud is aware of the scam, the sooner they can warn others and potentially take action.

Frequently asked questions

I received a call saying I've won a free holiday — is this a scam?

Almost certainly yes. Legitimate holiday companies do not cold-call people to offer free holidays or exclusive deals. If you did not enter a competition or sign up for a promotion, the call is almost certainly a scam designed to get you to attend a high-pressure sales presentation. Hang up and do not provide any personal information. If you are curious about the company, search for it online with the word 'scam' or check Companies House, but do not call the number they gave you.

What should I do if I've already signed a holiday club contract?

Contact your bank immediately and ask them to block any recurring payments to the company. Send a written request for a full refund to the company's registered address, citing your right to cancel within 14 days under consumer law. If they refuse or ignore you, contact your bank's dispute team and ask about a chargeback. Report the scam to Action Fraud (0300 123 2040) and keep all documents. Do not sign any additional paperwork or send more money.

Can I get my money back if I've already paid a holiday club?

It depends on how you paid and how long ago. If you paid by credit or debit card within the last 120 days, your bank can often recover the money through a chargeback if the company has not delivered what was promised. If you paid by bank transfer, recovery is harder but still possible if you can prove fraud — contact your bank's fraud team immediately. If the company is still operating and you paid within 14 days, you may have a legal right to cancel under consumer law. Contact Citizens Advice (0808 223 1133) for specific advice on your situation.

How can I tell if a holiday club company is legitimate?

Check if the company is registered at Companies House (companieshouse.gov.uk) and has a clear UK address and trading history. Search online for complaints and reviews — scams typically have numerous negative reviews about high-pressure sales and refusal to cancel. Check if they are a member of ABTA or ATOL, which are recognised travel industry bodies. Call the number on their official website (not a number given to you by a salesperson) and ask detailed questions about costs, cancellation terms, and available holidays. Be very wary of any company that pressures you to attend a presentation, demands upfront payment, or refuses to provide the full contract in writing before you commit.

What if the holiday club company is still charging me after I cancelled?

Contact your bank immediately and ask them to block the recurring payment or standing order. Send a written cancellation request to the company's registered address and keep a copy. If they continue to charge you, report this to Action Fraud (0300 123 2040) and ask your bank about a chargeback for unauthorised transactions. You can also contact Citizens Advice (0808 223 1133) for help pursuing a refund or small claims action. Document every charge and keep all correspondence with the company.
